en: He had neither son nor household.
There was no racehorse to ride into war.
They spoke his name over and over.
He stood between me and death.
The wicked enemy knew no mercy.
From the swarming Chinese host,
From its unbreakable iron net,
He rose from his misery to the height.
He seated Aitai above the rest.
His life was being carried away.
There was no immense, mighty hero.
My strength, dearer than life itself,
I reach out my hand and implore.
Chengker, the shriveled old woman,
Became bronze in China.
She was separated from China.
The remnant left to wander,
Saying, “Now I shall seize him,”
Chengker, who boasted of heroism,
Had bound them all.
She herself twisted his mouth shut.
Saving himself alone,
Thinking it equal to a solemn greeting,
He left him alone behind the cart,
The army stood in the distance,
His regret remained as life was cut short,
The spirit of Kenen appeared to him,
Grief cut through him like snow,
The struggle remained at the hilt,
A necklace rang against the sword,
He looked aside and asked,
Steel defended the lamb,
He was practiced in the work of the sword,
The defenders were seen,
With a pale battle cry from his lineage,
Iyger, harnessed beyond compare,
There is another at the left-hand iron,
God is present at the saddle blanket,
Warriors without racehorses,
Would he come without riding so?
At last, saying, This is it,
Freedom together with death,
He did not count it equal in his eyes,
That boundless feat of courage,
His own mind prepared him,
The champion could not gain victory,
He grasped and swung his sword,
He halted there without a shield,
At some wretched Kalmak,
He struck and sent it across the neck,
The whistling sword reached him,
Iron-hard flesh of the neck,
Dark blood streamed and throbbed,
The head raised like a felt tent,
Fell to the ground with a thud,
Chyntemir laughed at what had happened.
That Üytkör had died,
The wrathful Chongteñir saw it,
From across the whole world of the Manchu,
The dun horse beneath him,
He rode it plunging onward,
The mace-bearer shouted,
Calling his great champion,
One eagle, countless falcons,
The dear Chinese host surged on,
“Charge, my dun horse,” he said,
Saying to weary the earth by riding,
The greatest spear in all the world,
The great spear wielded by Ebegey,
He shouted toward the Chinese,
Calling a champion from the Kayyñ,
Calling his countless champions,
Aker the warrior stirred great conflict,
His khan gave the command,
He saw they would not stand without charging,
The Chinese advanced, countless champions,
From nameless Kenen,
Together they destroyed his stratagem,
Chongteñir gathered his strength,
Saying the heart’s root had broken,
Saying your passing was truly death,
Calling the spoil a dream,
Even if you had a thousand lives,
Saying this blow would carry you away,
Turning the speech of the myriad host,
His eyes blazed from the center,
He tightened the cords of his coat,
He struck with the spear,
Both a champion and a lion-hearted hero.
Loosen his brow,
To Kenen, keenest of all,
My brave one grasped the sword,
Without letting the spear strike too deeply,
He found the true opening,
My valiant people, the white-capped Kyrgyz,
Of the forefather who passed beyond,
The compassion of my people,
Pleading with his ancestral spirit,
He would split the hero's breast,
The hero turned it at the midpoint,
And struck the spear apart,
After the spear had broken,
When he was left alone behind the cart,
From Kenen in the contest,
The ember flared on the campaign,
Again he sharpened himself for the warrior's company,
Perhaps Chyntemir could not prevail,
Against the pleading Kalmak,
Both ears were firm,
Calling it hide from the sacred mane,
Calling it inward from the neck,
Calling it the work that opens your face,
Making the pale land into a hero's field,
Distracted, we made the ravager a hero,
Parted from the gray racehorse,
Why did we spill blood before us?
Blood flowed from the dark eyes,
Raging onward in blood,
His dear eyes turned blue,
Hero Kenen grew wrathful,
The camel-cutting sword at his waist,
The pale musket above his head.
Pleading with Kudurek,
Gathering what he had cut down, he throbbed with pain,
The unfound treasure rang out,
If God allowed it, that precious life,
Drawing hope and placing trust,
Biting clean through his lip,
Dear hero who could never be sated,
How wrathful Chyntemir proved,
At the very place where he laid his hand,
Sharpening it thoroughly against iron,
His sorrowful eyes flashed,
He drew out his sword,
Hero Kenen's gray racehorse,
The hero ground it down from the top,
He pulled and sent the blow,
Kalmak and Muslim alike,
Never forgetting the tears behind his eyes,
Kyrgyz champions upon the road,
To make sport of the nearby Kalmak,
To recount what had befallen,
Hero Kenen reached for the sword,
Turning back to strike with the sword,
O, of the warrior Chyntemir,
His true racehorse struck,
His house-sized head fell,
Like a mountain collapsing,
Now may God take the one who fired,
When the enemy Chyntemir remained,
His elder brother, dear Kokzhal the hero,
Twisting aside beneath the sword,
In grief he raised a fierce cry,
The sword named Koyron stopped,
Its blade remained in his hand.
At that time Chongteñir,
Stood rigid without moving on,
He could not make a single move,
Unable to return from the repeated assault,
Kenen alone who had grappled with them,
The Kyrgyz rescued him,
They hurried toward the refuge,
Today the Kyrgyz had no rest,
They had no leader who girded his waist,
He surrendered his sword at the seal,
No wise Kyrgyz host remained,
Among the countless heroes named,
An army stood behind him,
Their champions fought,
The iron rope was drawn tight,
All became an iron host,
The Kyrgyz remained together,
The warrior who came out enraged,
When the brave man died there,
The Kyrgyz turned back,
The many people understood,
Do not return him to the youths,
The mount of Chongteñir,
They mounted his khan upon a hero,
China’s new racing horse,
Then Kenen,
His eyes like mountains, his teeth bright,
Such a soul born among men,
The dear champion arrived,
The iron rope was drawn tight,
Those around him attacked,
The eyes of the Chinese narrowed,
They truly lost the pale road.
They bound his hands fast.
Poor Kenen, the lion,
The champion who girded his waist,
My strength, the Kyrgyz hero,
The one ordained by Almighty God,
The one who loved the white-capped people.
Kenen stood alone with God.
They devastated what stood assembled,
Making their great violence known,
And burning the soul with its truth.
They summoned the Kalmyk to grapple.
He rebuked them in his wrath.
They twisted his white arms behind his waist.
Test the whole body and bind it tight.
They fastened the restraint they had made.
They forced his supple waist to bend.
They drove him toward the gray Kalmyks.
Before all the countless Chinese,
They left him with teeth of humiliation.
They had him bound in disgrace.
They made his two eyes spread wide.
They bound him before the many Kalmyks.
They trampled and plundered him.
Saying, “He avenged your forefather,”
They had the wrestlers beat him.
Then they drove him before their khan.
The cruel, cold, dark night,
Poor Kenen saw it.
His two hands were bound,
While his two golden eyes still shone.
They bound him tight before the khan.
They brought him down to the promenade.
To the golden-covered platform,
Before the hero Chengker,
They dragged him forward and did this.
Baimyrza, the dear champion,
Perhaps there were four at that place,
At the end of the appointed age,
Captured and brought low,
To the warrior Kenen the hero,
Crossing his path, he began to speak,
Twisting his face and casting venom,
He laid a heavy hardship upon him,
To the words I have spoken,
Will you submit, Kenen?
The day when discord is cast,
Will you surrender, hero Kenen?
After speaking without drawing back,
Will you die, hero Kenen?
A people burdened by black grief,
I will not submit to what he says,
It is the land my people have seen,
I will not give you to China,
I am the dark-eyed one among warriors,
Cut off my head right now,
I am the one who stood in defiance,
I have no waist firmly girded,
Taking the hand offered in surrender,
This world seen since the dawn is firm,
If he is a warrior, he will be a champion,
If Kongurbai's ancient fame remains,
My hand can hold a little longer,
I shall know the warrior's worth,
Let my mother ask for my head,
Steel is in my hand,
My answer came silently from Aktan,
When the tormented victim stood there,
How could they bind his feet at the waist?
